newsitem.title: GERMANY: Toepfer sees global wheat stocks falling in 97/98.
newsitem.headline: Toepfer sees global wheat stocks falling in 97/98.

text.p: Grain trader Alfred C Toepfer said world wheat stocks should be drawn down in the 1997/98 year against a background of stable production and rising import demand.
The trader in its monthly market report pegged the global grain crop in 1997 at 580 million tonnes, unchanged from 1996, but forecast consumption to rise by three to four million tonnes.
"This scenario looks likely to keep world wheat prices at high levels in 1997/98," Toepfer said.
"This means that export restitutions in the European Union and the United States, if applied at all, look set to be quite limited," Toepfer said.
India was forecast to raise wheat imports by one million tonnes over 1996/97 to three million in the new season.
Iraq should step up its foreign purchases by 500,000 tonnes to two million and Iran was expected to import at least the same amount as in 1996/97 -- six million tonnes.
Unfavourable weather in North Africa may increase the region's wheat import requirements while imports by Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines were also seen rising.
Toepfer forecast global wheat trade volumes in 1997/98 at 94-95 million tonnes, up three to four million from 1996/97.
Exaggerated fears of wheat crop reductions in the U.S. had been overridden by latest government data, Toepfer said.
The EU should harvest a normal wheat crop after rainfall since the end of April outweighed earlier fears of drought damage.
But Canada, Argentina and Australia had reduced their wheat areas in favour of oilseeds and this would contribute to global tightness.
Toepfer pegged the 1997 EU wheat crop at just under 91 million tonnes, the same level as in 1996, based on a one percent area expansion.
EU durum wheat output could fall to seven million tonnes from 7.5 million previously because the area was down four percent, it added.
World wheat stocks at the end of 1996/97 were forecast three million tonnes higher than a year earlier at 98 million tonnes, but historically that remained a low level.
